History & Mission

The foundation of geotechnical knowledge in America

USUCGER was born during the 1985 San Francisco International Conference on Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering, to preserve an important source of research funding for the geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental community — NSF's program in the Directorate of Engineering. The first national meeting followed in Houston, Texas in 1986.

The 1991 Arlington meeting set the long-range course and built lasting coalitions with ASFE, ASCE-GED and ADSC. Today USUCGER is the primary collective voice for geotechnical engineering education and research in U.S. universities.

It is USUCGER's mission to provide advocacy for the continued development and expansion of high quality geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering research and education which will enhance the welfare of humankind and meet the needs of the nation.
Long-Term Objectives
1
Become a strong and effective advocate for funding of innovative geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental research and development through proper representation at federal, state and industrial/private agencies.
2
Be a forum for members in gathering and disseminating information on funding opportunities and the results of completed research and development projects.
3
Foster cooperation with other organizations with common goals in identifying R&D needs and providing unified representation in expanding the funding base.
4
Effect long-term positive change in the funding of civil engineering research and development through legislation, by involving the construction industry directly in the funding process.

About USUCGER

History & Mission

USUCGER was born at the 1985 San Francisco International Conference on Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering, to preserve and grow research funding for the geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental community.

Read the By-Laws →Meet the Board

History of USUCGER

The United States Universities Council on Geotechnical Education and Research (USUCGER) was born during the 1985 San Francisco International Conference on Soil Mechanics and Foundation Engineering, in order to preserve an important source of research funding to the geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental community — that is, NSF's program in these areas in the Directorate of Engineering.

The first national meeting of USUCGER took place in Houston, Texas in 1986 with funding from NSF, which led to formal organization and development of the constitution.

The second meeting of USUCGER in Arlington, Texas in 1991 has become an extremely effective means of looking into the future and setting the long-range course, as well as defining specific attainable objectives for the coming years. A strategic plan was formulated for 1992–1997 based on ideas developed by the working groups organized during that meeting.

In the same meeting, USUCGER began to build strong coalitions and official liaisons with other organizations with compatible goals.

Mission

It is USUCGER's mission to provide advocacy for the continued development and expansion of high quality geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering research and education which will enhance the welfare of humankind and meet the needs of the nation.

Long-term objectives

1
To become a strong and effective advocate for funding of innovative geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental research and development through proper representation at federal, state and industrial/private agencies.
2
To be a forum for its members in gathering and disseminating information regarding funding opportunities and results of completed research and development projects in the geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental areas.
3
To foster cooperation with other organizations with common goals in coordinating efforts in identifying research and development needs, and providing unified representation in expanding the funding base and resources.
4
To effect long-term positive changes in funding of civil engineering research and development through legislation, by involving the construction industry directly in the funding process.

Composition of the organization

USUCGER has over 100 dues-paying institutional geotechnical engineering member programs with additional international representatives — today the member universities list runs to more than 180 institutions. The email list reaches approximately 300 members throughout the nation and abroad.

USUCGER currently receives financial support from Member University dues. The USUCGER Board is comprised of elected members from the geotechnical faculty pool across the nation, with four senior and four junior directors serving staggered four-year terms as set out in the By-Laws.

Governance

USUCGER By-Laws

Eleven articles governing the purpose, membership, board, officers and committees of the Council. Use the contents panel to jump to any article.

About this document
These by-laws govern the United States Universities Council on Geotechnical Education and Research. Amendments require a two-thirds vote of the delegates voting, and must be circulated at least thirty days beforehand and discussed at a Council meeting (Article IX).
Article I

Purpose

The United States Universities Council on Geotechnical Education and Research, hereinafter referred to as USUCGER, is a non-profit organization of universities actively engaged in education and research in the field of geotechnical engineering. It is organized for the purpose of concerted action in whatever way may be desirable for the encouragement of geotechnical education and research.

The Council will:

  • Foster cooperation, exchanges of ideas and findings, and dissemination of data among universities.
  • Organize meetings from time to time, as may be appropriate, to discuss geotechnical research and educational issues.
  • Provide a forum through which contacts may be developed with the purposes of stimulating increased interest in research and cooperation between universities, public and private research funding agencies, engineering societies, private companies, industries and other interested parties.
  • Establish a mechanism through which the collection of views of the academic research community can be coordinated and expressed as may seem appropriate in the national interest.
  • Foster cooperation and exchange of ideas among geotechnical engineering educators and researchers.
Article II

Scope

The scope of USUCGER includes all aspects of (a) basic and applied research in geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering and geomechanics, (b) related interdisciplinary areas important for use and improvement of available theories and techniques as well as for any future developments and applications, and (c) educational programs at all levels (K–12 through graduate programs, and including the general public) in geotechnical engineering.

Article III

Membership

Section 1 — Qualifications

Academic institutions in the United States that have a program of research and/or education in geotechnical engineering shall be eligible for membership in the Council. Applications for membership are subject to the approval of the Board of Directors. Application for membership shall be forwarded to the Executive Secretary under the signature of the contact member of the institution seeking membership, and shall include a description of the institution's present programs and future plans in undergraduate and graduate research and education in geotechnical engineering. Other relevant information such as course descriptions, number of students, research projects, and type of research (basic/applied or practice-oriented) may be described in the membership application.

Section 2 — Delegates and voting

Each member institution shall designate a delegate who has voting rights. The delegate can designate a proxy within their institution if they are unable to take part in voting.

Section 3 — Voting

Each member institution shall have two (2) votes that will be exercised electronically by the delegate(s) or an alternate designated by one of the delegates. A single delegate shall cast votes for the institution represented. The voting delegate may cast one vote for a junior faculty candidate (who shall be an Assistant Professor at the time of nomination) and one vote for a senior faculty candidate (who shall be an Associate or Full Professor). No proxy votes shall be allowed.

Section 4 — Affiliates

Foreign universities, corporations or individuals engaged in geotechnical engineering may be associated with the Council as affiliates upon approval of the Board of Directors. Affiliate status is non-voting. Each affiliate shall designate one representative who will serve as liaison representative with the Council.

Section 5 — Withdrawal of membership

A member may withdraw from the Council upon written notice to the Board of Directors.

Section 6 — Removal from membership

An institution shall cease to be a voting member upon failure to pay dues by the end of the membership year.

Article IV

Functions

Section 1 — Council activities

Functions of the Council shall include such activities as listed herein and other activities that may be approved by a majority of voting delegates. In performing its functions, the Council may use the services of any qualified person whether or not such person is a delegate of the Council.

  • To represent the university community in activities aimed at encouraging the growth of research and education in geotechnical engineering on a broad, interdisciplinary basis.
  • To provide and disseminate the information necessary for adequate understanding of the status of education and research in geotechnical engineering.
  • To inform members of the Council on matters of importance relating to geotechnical engineering.
  • To organize seminars, symposia, conferences, etc., from time to time as may be appropriate, to present the results of ongoing research and educational programs to the academic community and others, with a view to minimizing undesirable duplication of effort and optimizing the efficiency of academic research resources.
  • To provide a forum through which industrial contacts may be developed with a view to stimulating increased cooperation between universities, engineering companies and government agencies, and increased private funding in the geotechnical research and education field.
  • To establish an organization through which the collection of views of the academic research community in geotechnical engineering can be coordinated and expressed as may seem appropriate in the national interest.
  • To establish liaison with other bodies or groups which have research interests in areas having significance to geotechnical engineering, including rock mechanics, dynamics of porous materials, flow through porous media, mass transport, geological engineering, mining engineering, pavement analysis, geophysics, environmental geotechnics, ice mechanics, materials engineering and expert systems.
  • To conduct programs for the purpose of encouraging students to enter fields of education and research related to geotechnical engineering.
  • To serve as a clearinghouse for information on faculty vacancies and available personnel.
  • To coordinate visits of distinguished foreign visitors.
  • To establish standing committees by majority vote of the Council.
Section 2 — Scope

It is understood that the Council will not:

  • Act as an accrediting agency or make comparative ratings of member institutions.
  • Attempt to standardize curricula.
  • Act as a referee on research proposals or other requests for grants for other organizations.
  • Solicit funds in support of research for disbursement to member institutions.
  • Assume the responsibility for the publication of technical periodicals.
  • Participate or intervene in (including the publishing or distribution of statements) any political campaign on behalf of a candidate for public office.
  • Expend a substantial part of its activities in attempting to influence legislation.
Article V

Meetings

Section 1 — Schedule

An annual business meeting of the Council shall be held, with the date and place selected by the Board of Directors. Special meetings may be convened by the Board of Directors to consider matters of extreme importance. A meeting agenda shall be distributed prior to meetings.

Section 2 — Location

The annual business meeting will typically be held at the annual ASCE Geo-Congress, sponsored by the Geo-Institute, so as to maximize attendance and minimize yearly scheduling, planning efforts and budget concerns. Holding the regular meeting at the Geo-Congress in the first quarter of the year is also beneficial in terms of scheduling the nomination and election process, and providing a clear start and stop to term limits. Other venues for the annual meeting may be considered, but priority should be given to events where the majority of the Board will likely be in attendance. In addition to the annual meeting, there should be at least one conference call (more if necessary to plan upcoming events) held during the year to keep the Board of Directors on task and moving forward.

Article VI

Board of Directors

Section 1 — Number, term and qualifications

The Board of Directors shall consist of eight delegates elected for a term of four years each, plus the Past-President as an ex-officio member without voting privileges. Four members of the Board shall be junior (untenured) to represent young researchers, and four senior. Directors serve in rotation, two being elected each year to replace retiring members of the Board; each year, one junior and one senior board member is elected.

It is anticipated that delegates will spend the first year becoming familiar with the organization and its activities, the second and third years in leadership positions, and the final year transitioning leadership to newer members of the group. The change in Board membership occurs at the annual Board of Directors meeting, typically held in the first quarter of the year. A delegate may serve two successive full terms but may not be re-elected thereafter until the second annual meeting following his or her service as director. Only one delegate from any member institution may serve on the Board at any given time. Vacancies on the Board may be filled on an interim basis as described in Section 4 below.

Section 2 — Election
  • A nominating committee (as specified in Section 4 of this Article) shall designate a minimum of four nominees chosen from among the delegates for each annual election of two Board members — two junior and two senior. Nominations shall be announced to the members by September 30 and additional nominations solicited. Nominations close on October 30 and elections are held. The Executive Secretary then asks member institution delegates to cast their votes on the nominees by December 1. Votes are tallied and new Board members notified at least six weeks in advance of the first Board meeting of the next calendar year, so as to make proper arrangements to attend if the meeting is not by teleconference.
  • Each member institution shall have two (2) votes that can be exercised electronically by the delegate(s) or the alternates in the absence of one or both delegates. A single delegate may cast votes for the institution represented. One vote should be for the junior faculty and one for the senior faculty position.
  • The nominee for each position receiving the highest number of votes cast will be elected to the Board. Ties shall be broken by a secret ballot of the Board of Directors.
Section 3 — Meetings

The Board of Directors shall meet at such times and places as designated by the President, including via teleconference. The President or any three members of the Board may call a meeting of the Board. Immediately following the annual meeting of the Council, the incoming and outgoing Boards shall meet in joint session.

Section 4 — Functions

The Board of Directors shall have the following functions, and such other functions as may be assigned to it by majority vote of all delegates designated by the member institutions:

  • To elect a President from its membership for a term of two years. A Board member in their fourth year of a term is not eligible to be elected President.
  • To appoint the chairman, vice-chairman and members of standing committees.
  • To appoint a Secretary/Treasurer and determine the conditions of their appointment. The position need not be an elected Board member.
  • To approve the appointment of other committees or subcommittees, which have a life of one year that may be extended annually as needed.
  • To establish standards and criteria for admission to membership in conformance with Article III, Section 1, and to review and act upon applications for membership.
  • To coordinate activities as proper functions of the Council.
  • To call meetings of all delegates to the Council as necessary to conduct the business of the Council, and to establish quorums and other rules for governing meetings.
  • To prepare and submit to delegates — at meetings or by mail ballot — issues of policy which require a decision of the Council, and to execute the decisions of the Council. Policies that impinge on pending legislation require a decision of the Council.
  • To report promptly to delegates on important actions taken on behalf of the Council.
  • To receive and disburse funds on behalf of the Council.
  • To approve the employment of necessary staff, purchase of supplies and equipment, and publication of such material as necessary.
  • To make interim appointments to vacancies on the Board of Directors. Replacements made by reason of resignation, or replacement of a member as a delegate, shall be for the duration of the unexpired term of the Board member replaced. For Board members on leave, the replacement shall be for the period of leave.
  • To designate a nominating committee to nominate candidates for regular vacancies on the Board of Directors and make such other nominations as may be requested. The nominating committee shall consist of five members, three of whom shall not be members or immediate past members of the Board; at least one member shall be a junior faculty member. Nominees proposed shall reflect the geographic distribution, research areas and educational activities of the Council.
  • To invite individuals to attend Council meetings as observers.
  • To approve the annual budget.
Article VII

Officers

Section 1 — Number

The officers of the Council shall consist of a President, a Secretary, a Treasurer, a Comptroller and a Webmaster, each elected or appointed by the Board of Directors as specified in Article VI, Section 4. Such other officers and assistant officers as may be deemed necessary may be elected or appointed by the Board of Directors.

Section 2 — President

The President shall be elected from among the Board members at the meeting immediately following the annual business meeting of the Council, by a procedure agreed upon by the Board members.

Section 3 — Secretary / Treasurer

The offices of Secretary and Treasurer shall be filled by appointment of the Board of Directors and may be combined. If the Secretary/Treasurer is not an elected Board member, they shall be an ex-officio non-voting Board member. The Treasurer shall prepare an annual budget and financial statement for approval by the Board at the annual meeting.

Section 4 — Comptroller

An elected member of the USUCGER Board, appointed by the Board, serving as the head accounting officer for USUCGER and responsible for financial oversight and planning.

Section 5 — Webmaster

The Webmaster serves at the request of the Board as an ex-officio non-voting Board member. The Webmaster is a paid position whose role is to keep the website up to date, help facilitate web-based activities such as dues payment and inquiries, and ensure that the online presence of USUCGER is accessible and relevant. The Board shall decide compensation.

Article VIII

Standing Committees

Section 1 — Establishment and membership

Standing committees of the Council may be established by a majority vote of the Board. The Board of Directors shall establish the membership of each standing committee. Members may be any qualified member of the Council.

Section 2 — Chairman and vice-chairman

Appointments of standing committee officers shall be made by the President with the concurrence of the Board of Directors for a four-year period, with privilege of succession. The Chairman and/or Vice-Chairman serves at the pleasure of the Board of Directors.

Section 3 — Management group

A management group shall be established for each standing committee and shall include the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, three other members of the committee, and the Board contact person as an ex-officio member.

Section 4 — Membership of management group

Prior to the annual business meeting of the Council, each committee will make recommendations to the Board of Directors for the Chairman, Vice-Chairman and members of the management group for the coming year. In general, membership of the management group will change each year, with the old chairman going off and one new member coming on.

Section 5 — Responsibilities

Standing committees shall provide continuous surveillance and review of fundamental aspects of university education and research in geotechnical engineering. They shall recommend programs for action to the Council or to the Board of Directors as appropriate, and shall carry out such tasks as may be requested.

Section 6 — Reports

Standing committees shall report to the Council at the annual meeting, and at Board meetings at the request of the Board of Directors.

Section 7 — Subcommittees

Subcommittees may be appointed by the standing committee subject to the approval of the Board of Directors.

Section 8 — Action

The chairmen of the standing committees shall report to the Board of Directors concerning the activities of their respective committees. The Board of Directors shall arrange for a mail ballot on committee recommendations as may be required by Article VI, Section 4.

Article IX

Amendments

Section 1 — Vote

These by-laws may be amended by a two-thirds vote of the delegates voting.

Section 2 — Propositions

Amendments may be proposed by any delegate to the Board of Directors or to the assembled Council.

Section 3 — Approval

The Board shall circulate the proposed amendment to all delegates at least thirty days prior to a vote. In addition, all amendments must be discussed at a Council meeting prior to a vote by the delegates.

Article X

Dues

The Board of Directors shall establish annual dues for members with the concurrence of two-thirds of the voting delegates. Proposed changes to the annual dues shall be brought forth at the annual business meeting of the Council.

Current dues and payment options →

Article XI

Reporting

The Board of Directors shall report on the activities of the Council at the annual business meeting, and issue special bulletins and reports as deemed necessary.

Join the USUCGER Community

Participation of all people with a vested interest in geotechnical research and teaching is encouraged. Current cycle: January 2025 – December 2027 at $75 per person.

Purchase University Membership →Purchase Associate Membership →

Not getting our emails?

How membership works

Payment is made in three-year increments. Whichever category you fall into, the dues are the same — $75 per person for the full cycle — and they are not prorated, so joining partway through a cycle costs the same as joining at the start.

Choosing your category

Category A (U.S. Universities) is for people affiliated with a U.S. academic institution that has a geotechnical research or education program. Each member institution designates a contact person, who must be a paid member; that contact person is also the institution's delegate for Council voting, and may sponsor graduate students.

Category B (Associates) is for everyone else with a stake in the field — faculty at non-U.S. institutions, consultants and practitioners, agency staff, and retired members of the community. Associate membership is a single seat and is non-voting.

What happens after you pay

  • You are added to the USUCGER email list, which reaches roughly 300 members in the U.S. and abroad.
  • Your name and affiliation appear in the public membership directory.
  • Your institution appears on the member universities list with you as the contact, if you are the designated contact person.
  • Your students become eligible to apply for travel grants, and you become eligible to nominate colleagues for awards.

Institutional membership rules

Under the By-Laws, academic institutions in the United States with a program of research and/or education in geotechnical engineering are eligible for Council membership, subject to approval of the Board of Directors. Each member institution designates a delegate with voting rights, and holds two votes — one to be cast for a junior faculty candidate and one for a senior faculty candidate in Board elections. An institution ceases to be a voting member on failure to pay dues by the end of the membership year.

Questions

Membership, dues and directory questions go to the Membership Coordinator or the webmaster at webmaster@usucger.org. See the contact page for the full list of addresses.

Home/Activities/Student Travel Grants
Student Support

Student Travel Grants

Up to $1,000 per student toward airfare, hotel, per diem and conference registration for students presenting accepted research, advised by a USUCGER member. Two upcoming application cycles.

Download application info →

The award

The USUCGER Board sponsors students — graduate or undergraduate — to attend conferences in support of their accepted research. Awards are up to $1,000 per student and may be used for airfare, hotel, per diem and/or conference student registration fees.

The Board will evaluate applications during two upcoming cycles and anticipates granting at least one travel award per cycle, depending on available funding. Separate solicitations are emailed by the USUCGER Board for each cycle. The award supports travel to geotechnical, geoenvironmental-focused or interdisciplinary conferences.

Deadlines

Conference datesApplication deadlineAnticipated notification
Jan 1 – Apr 30, 2027 (this cycle)November 15, 2026December 15, 2026
May 1 – Aug 31, 2027 (next cycle)March 15, 2027April 15, 2027

Apply to the cycle that covers your conference dates, not the cycle you happen to be in when you apply.

How to apply

  1. Download the current call (January 1 – April 30, 2027 conferences) for the full instructions.
  2. Confirm your advisor's USUCGER membership is current for the 2025–2027 cycle — if not, they can renew here. Each member may nominate one student per cycle.
  3. Prepare a single PDF named LastName.pdf with your advisor's signed letter, a CV (up to three pages), a one-page essay, an itemized travel budget and the submitted abstract, plus a recorded video of up to three minutes summarizing your research.
  4. Submit the package through the online application form by 11:59 PM Pacific on the deadline for your cycle. Advisors may send their letter separately through this form.

Questions? Email the Board at uboard@usucger.org.

Download application info (PDF) →

Finding a conference

The conference list carries geotechnical events shared by USUCGER members, and a more comprehensive international list is maintained by ISSMGE.

Browse conferences →

Maximum award per student
Based on actual costs: airfare (main cabin), baggage fees, lodging (single room), conference registration, airport transportation, and meals and incidentals up to $60/day with itemized receipts. Reimbursed after the conference.

Activities

Small Research Grants

USUCGER seed funding for projects that improve how geotechnical engineering is taught. Every funded project delivers free, reusable material for the whole community.

Funded Projects

What the grants have produced

Every funded project delivers something the whole community can use — activity libraries, physical demonstrations, video series and open-source software. All of it is free.

🏗
Geotechnical Education Modelers (GEMs)
2020–2021   Dr. Fawad Niazi · Purdue University Fort Wayne · $5,000 from USUCGER
A two-year project developing physical educational models for soil–structure interaction, co-funded by CELT ($2,500) and the CME Department ($4,000). Two video walkthroughs document the models and how to use them in class.
Video part 1 → Video part 2 →
✨
Soil Magic 2.0
2017–2018   Dr. Hoyoung Seo · Texas Tech University
Eight classroom demonstration activities designed to produce “aha” moments in soil mechanics, each paired with a video demonstration and a learning module.
Project report (PDF) →
🤝
Active Learning Activities for Undergraduate Soil Mechanics
2016–2017   Dr. Kristin Sample-Lord (Villanova) & Dr. Gretchen Bohnhoff (UW–Platteville)
Sixteen group activities in editable formats, each with an instructor summary sheet, learning objectives, handout, solution set, example rubric and supplemental information. Activities run from one to fifty minutes.
Download the library → Give feedback → See on teaching aids →
💻
geotech — Geotechnical Engineering Software Package in R
2014–2015   Dr. James Kaklamanos · Merrimack College
A free R package covering phase diagrams and index parameters, grain-size distributions, plasticity, classification, compaction, groundwater, subsurface stresses, Mohr circles, consolidation, shear strength, bearing capacity, lateral earth pressures, slope stability and subsurface exploration.
Package on CRAN → Software page → Final report (PDF) → Presentation (PDF) →

Resources & Media

Teaching Aids

Free, classroom-ready material contributed by the USUCGER community and allied organizations — activities, modules, course notes, exam banks and lab demonstrations.

🧩
Library of Group Activities Promoting Active Learning in Undergraduate Soil Mechanics
Sixteen different activities developed with the help of undergraduate students. Each activity includes an instructor summary sheet with learning objectives and instructions, the activity handout, the solution set, an example rubric and supplemental information. Activities range from one or two minutes up to fifty minutes.
Download the library → Funded by a USUCGER grant →
🧠
Geotech CAT-Apps for Building Critical Thinking Skills
Thirteen CAT-App questions, each with a problem statement and three to four prompts. Anticipated student responses are supplied for every question in three categories — strong, average and weak — so you can calibrate discussion and grading.
Open the question set →
✨
Soil Magic 2.0 — classroom demonstrations
Eight classroom demonstration activities with accompanying videos and learning modules, developed at Texas Tech University to create “aha” moments in soil mechanics.
Report & activity table (PDF) → Project details →
🏗
Geotechnical Education Modelers (GEMs)
Physical models for teaching soil–structure interaction, developed at Purdue University Fort Wayne with USUCGER support. Two videos document construction and classroom use.
Part 1 → Part 2 →
📚
USUCGER 2020 Geotechnical Engineering Faculty Teaching Strategies & Resources Workshop
Workshop report and materials aimed at helping geotechnical faculty at all career stages become more effective and efficient teachers, plus a bank of exam questions and solutions contributed by participants for use in undergraduate geo-engineering courses.
Report & materials (PDF) → Exam problems (PDF) →
🌍
Introductory Course on Geoenvironmental Engineering
Resources to prepare you to teach an introductory geoenvironmental engineering course: challenges in teaching the subject, relevant course content, a course syllabus, teaching resources (textbook, homework questions, projects and exams) and example lecture slides.
Course resources → Contact: kreddy@uic.edu
🌴
Course Notes: Dynamic Response of Soil and Soil-Foundation Systems
Full lecture notes for RPI CIVL 6540, addressed mostly to geotechnical and structural master's and PhD students.
Open the notes → Contact: zeghal@rpi.edu
♻
Introductory Course on Sustainable Engineering
A short course addressing the growing urgency of incorporating sustainability into engineering curricula. It covers current challenges, presents the content of a new textbook, and offers guidance on selecting topics and preparing a syllabus.
Course resources → Contact: kreddy@uic.edu
🎥
Recorded lecture courses
A complete 26-lecture introductory geotechnical engineering course, chapter-by-chapter webcasts aligned to Coduto, Yeung & Kitch, and a full soil mechanics laboratory on video.
Go to videos & webinars →
🦠
Biogeotechnics Education & Outreach Materials
The NSF-funded Center for Bio-mediated and Bio-inspired Geotechnics (CBBG) has developed a series of biogeotechnics modules for K–12 and university use, including a PowerPoint lesson for introductory civil engineering courses and 36 lesson plans developed by K–12 teachers.
Intro module (PPTX) → K–12 lesson plans →
🗺
Engineering Geology and Site Characterization Educational Resources
Six modules covering engineering geology, rock properties and engineering characterization, site characterization, geologic mapping and geologic hazards — plus an SPT video and PowerPoint slides.
Open the modules →
🌱
Introduction to Geosynthetics
Four short video presentations making up a one-hour introductory lecture, giving students an overview of geosynthetics, their types and their functions. Delivered by Professor Jorge G. Zornberg, University of Texas at Austin, with a companion site for educators.
For students → For educators →
🎓
Science Education Resource Center (Carleton College)
An extensive collection of online teaching resources and peer-reviewed activities that can be incorporated into geotechnical engineering, geology, geohazards and earthquake engineering courses.

Home/Resources/Software & Data
Resources & Media

Software & Data

Directories, open-source packages, virtual laboratories and experimental databases for geotechnical teaching and research.

📂
Geotechnical & Geoenvironmental Software Directory (GGSD)
Catalogues more than 1,700 programs across geotechnical engineering, soil mechanics, rock mechanics, engineering geology, foundation engineering, hydrogeology, geoenvironmental and environmental engineering, data analysis and data visualisation. The best first stop when you need to know what exists for a given problem.
Browse the directory →
📈
geotech — Geotechnical Engineering Software Package in R
A free, open-source R package developed with USUCGER support. It performs phase-diagram and index parameter calculations, grain-size distributions, plasticity and soil classification, compaction, groundwater, subsurface stresses, Mohr circle analyses, consolidation settlement and rate, shear strength, bearing capacity, lateral earth pressures, slope stability and subsurface exploration.
Package on CRAN → Software information → Final report (PDF) → Presentation (PDF) →
🖥
Virtual Simulator for Advanced Geotechnical Laboratory Testing
A browser-based simulator that lets students set up and run advanced laboratory tests without tying up laboratory equipment — useful for pre-lab preparation, large sections and remote teaching.
Open the simulator →
📊
Case Western element test database
Over 234 tests conducted on three different sands in dense and loose conditions, plus the results of 18 tests on Edgar Plastic Kaolin clay and 8 tests on Hydrite 121 clay. Researchers can use the database to validate constitutive relations; it also makes an excellent source of real data for student projects.
Open the database →
🛠 Software from USUCGER grants
The geotech R package came out of a USUCGER small research grant. Past funded projects and their deliverables are listed on the small research grants page.

Home/Resources/Funding Tips
Resources & Media

Funding Tips

Practical pointers on finding and winning research funding, to help early career geotechnical faculty compete well.

Finding funding for geotechnical engineering research

This page offers practical pointers to help early career geotechnical engineering faculty compete successfully for research funding.

📄 An updated guide is planned
The Council's earlier Do's and Don'ts funding guide has been retired because it was out of date. The Board is considering preparing an updated version; it will be posted here and announced on the USUCGER email list when available.

Where geotechnical research money comes from

USUCGER exists in part because of NSF's program in geomechanical, geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering in the Directorate of Engineering — preserving that funding source was the reason the Council was founded in 1985. Advocacy for research funding at federal, state and industrial/private agencies remains the first of the Council's long-term objectives.

Beyond NSF, the community draws on state DOT research programs, federal agencies with infrastructure and hazards missions, and industry partners. Announcements of funding opportunities circulate on the USUCGER email list, so keeping your membership current is the simplest way to hear about them early.

Getting the most out of this

  • Read the program solicitation closely before you draft — most of the recurring problems are structural, not editorial.
  • Talk to a program officer early, before the proposal is written.
  • Ask a colleague who has served on a panel to read a draft. Panel experience is the single most useful thing to borrow.
  • Watch the list for calls, and give yourself more lead time than feels necessary.
💰 Funding at USUCGER
🎓 Small research grants ✈ Student travel grants 🏛 Advocacy & objectives
📩 Stay in the loop
Funding announcements go out on the USUCGER email list, which reaches around 300 members. If you are not receiving them, check spam first, then email webmaster@usucger.org.
✉ Add your experience
If you have advice from serving on a review panel or managing a program that would help early career colleagues, send it to the webmaster for inclusion.

Workshops

USUCGER-organized workshops for geotechnical faculty, and the materials they produced.

Past Workshops

Workshops and what they produced

USUCGER workshops are built around a deliverable the whole community can keep using afterwards. Everything below is free.

🎓
USUCGER Geotechnical Engineering Faculty Teaching Strategies & Resources Workshop
2020
A workshop aimed at helping geotechnical faculty at all career stages become more effective and efficient teachers. It produced a full report and materials package, plus a bank of exam questions and solutions contributed by participants for use in undergraduate geo-engineering courses.
Report & materials (PDF) → Exam problems (PDF) →
🌍
Teaching an Introductory Course on Geoenvironmental Engineering
A short course preparing attendees to teach an introductory geoenvironmental engineering course — challenges in teaching the subject, relevant content, a syllabus, teaching resources and example lecture slides.
Course materials → Contact: kreddy@uic.edu
♻
Teaching an Introductory Course on Sustainable Engineering
A short course on incorporating sustainability into engineering curricula: current challenges, the content of a new textbook, and guidance on selecting topics and preparing a syllabus.
Course materials → Contact: kreddy@uic.edu
